summary.text: A putative uniform constant is transferred, using bounded-relation-free integer weights and binary blocks \(a_i2^j\), to a dimension-independent positive lower bound on determinants of rational matrices whose zero-sum lifts send no nonzero integer vector into the open unit cube. For an odd cycle, \(I+\tfrac12P\) has determinant \(1+2^{-b}\) and the needed lattice-avoidance property; recursively composing this gadget to depth \(k\) and deleting its anchor produces such a matrix with determinant \(\frac{(1+2^{-b})^{\sum_{j<k}b^j}}{(3/2)^k}\), which can be made arbitrarily small by choosing \(k\) and then large odd \(b\).

full_proof.text:
We prove that no positive absolute constant with the asserted property exists.

Throughout, if \(I\) is a finite index set and \(a=(a_i)_{i\in I}\) is an integer or natural-number family, say that \(a\) is \(Q\)-relation-free if
\[
 \sum_{i\in I} a_i c_i=0,\qquad |c_i|<Q\quad(i\in I)
\]
forces every integer \(c_i\) to be zero.

Suppose, toward a contradiction, that there is a constant \(C>0\) such that whenever \(A\subseteq\{1,\dots,N\}\) has distinct subset sums, one has
\[
 C2^{|A|}<N. \tag{1}
\]
We will derive from (1) a dimension-independent positive lower bound for a class of lattice determinants, and then construct determinants in that class tending to zero.

## 1. Binary blocks

We first record the elementary way in which a relation-free family produces a set with distinct subset sums.

Let \(a_1,\dots,a_d\) be positive natural numbers, all at most \(W\), and suppose this family is \(2^k\)-relation-free, where \(k>0\). Consider
\[
 \mathcal A=\{a_i2^j:1\le i\le d,\ 0\le j<k\}. \tag{2}
\]
This is a set of \(dk\) distinct positive integers and it has distinct subset sums.

Here are the details. A signed binary sum
\[
 e_0+2e_1+\cdots+2^{k-1}e_{k-1},\qquad e_j\in\{-1,0,1\},
\]
has absolute value less than \(2^k\). Moreover, if it is zero, all its digits vanish: if the highest nonzero digit is in position \(m\), its absolute contribution is \(2^m\), whereas all lower contributions have total absolute value at most \(2^m-1\).

Suppose two subsets of the indexed collection in (2) have equal sums. Subtracting their incidence vectors gives coefficients \(e_{ij}\in\{-1,0,1\}\) and
\[
 0=\sum_i a_i\sum_{j=0}^{k-1}e_{ij}2^j.
\]
Put \(c_i=\sum_j e_{ij}2^j\). Then \(|c_i|<2^k\), so relation-freeness gives \(c_i=0\) for every \(i\). Uniqueness of the signed binary expansion then gives every \(e_{ij}=0\), proving equality of the two subsets. Applying this also to two singleton subsets shows that the indexed values in (2) are pairwise distinct, so \(|\mathcal A|=dk\).

Every element in (2) is at most
\[
 2^{k-1}W.
\]
Applying (1) to \(\mathcal A\), with \(d=r+1\), gives
\[
 C2^{(r+1)k}<2^{k-1}W\le 2^kW.
\]
After dividing by \(2^k\), we obtain the deliberately slightly weakened but useful estimate
\[
 C(2^k)^r<W. \tag{3}
\]
Thus any \(2^k\)-relation-free family of \(r+1\) positive natural numbers, all at most \(W\), must satisfy (3).

## 2. Cube-admissible rational matrices

For a rational \(r\times r\) matrix \(B\), define its zero-sum lift by
\[
 L(B)=\begin{pmatrix}B\\-\mathbf 1^TB\end{pmatrix}, \tag{4}
\]
an \((r+1)\times r\) matrix. Thus the first \(r\) coordinates of \(L(B)z\) are the coordinates of \(Bz\), and the last is minus their sum.

Call \(B\) cube-admissible if the only \(z\in\mathbb Z^r\) satisfying
\[
 |(Bz)_i|<1\quad(1\le i\le r),
 \qquad
 \left|\sum_{i=1}^r(Bz)_i\right|<1 \tag{5}
\]
is \(z=0\). Equivalently, using the sup norm, \(B\) is cube-admissible exactly when
\[
 \|L(B)z\|_\infty<1,\\ z\in\mathbb Z^r
 \quad\Longrightarrow\quad z=0. \tag{6}
\]

We next prove the central transfer statement.

**Transfer statement.** If \(B\) is a nonsingular cube-admissible rational \(r\times r\) matrix, then for every \(k\) there is an integer family
\[
 a^{(k)}=(a_0^{(k)},\dots,a_r^{(k)})

a^{(k)}=(a_0^{(k)},\dots,a_r^{(k)})
\]
which is \(2^k\)-relation-free and for which, for every fixed \(i\),
\[
 \frac{a_i^{(k)}}{(2^k)^r}\longrightarrow |\det B|. \tag{7}
\]
The entries in this statement are initially integers; by (7) they are positive for all sufficiently large \(k\).

We now establish this transfer statement.

Choose a positive common denominator \(D\) so that
\[
 A=DB
\]
is an integral matrix. Since \(B\) is nonsingular, so is \(A\). By integer diagonal reduction there are unimodular integral matrices \(P,W\) and positive integers \(s_1,\dots,s_r\) such that
\[
 AW=P\,\operatorname{diag}(s_1,\dots,s_r). \tag{8}
\]
The signs of the diagonal entries can be absorbed into \(W\), which explains why they may be taken positive. Taking absolute determinants in (8) gives
\[
 \prod_{i=1}^r s_i=|\det A|=D^r|\det B|. \tag{9}
\]
Let \(U=P^{-1}\), which is again integral.

For an integer parameter \(t\ge0\), consider the \((r+1)\times r\) bidiagonal matrix
\[
 C_t=
 \begin{pmatrix}
 ts_1&0&0&\cdots&0\\
 -1&ts_2&0&\cdots&0\\
 0&-1&ts_3&\cdots&0\\
 \vdots&&\ddots&\ddots&\vdots\\
 0&\cdots&0&-1&ts_r\\
 0&\cdots&0&0&-1
 \end{pmatrix}. \tag{10}
\]
Its columns are annihilated by the row vector
\[
 q_t=(1,\ ts_1,\ t^2s_1s_2,\dots,t^r s_1\cdots s_r). \tag{11}
\]
Indeed, this is just the recurrence saying that each entry in (11) is \(ts_i\) times its predecessor.

This annihilator is primitive, and more is true: the integral column span of \(C_t\) is the entire integral kernel of \(q_t\). To see this, delete the first row of \(C_t\). The resulting square matrix is triangular with all diagonal entries \(-1\), so it is unimodular. Given an integral \(c\) with \(q_t\cdot c=0\), one can therefore solve integrally for \(z\) so that the final \(r\) coordinates of \(C_tz\) equal those of \(c\). The first coordinates must then also agree, because both differences are annihilated by \(q_t\), whose first coefficient is \(1\). Hence
\[
 q_t\cdot c=0\quad\Longrightarrow\quad c=C_tz
 \text{ for some }z\in\mathbb Z^r. \tag{12}
\]

We now apply an integral shear corresponding to the changes of basis in (8). Define
\[
 S(U)=\begin{pmatrix}U&0\\ \mathbf 1^T&1\end{pmatrix}.
\]
There is an integral inverse shear \(T(P)\), because \(PU=I\), chosen so that \(T(P)S(U)=I\). Set
\[
 a(t)=S(U)^Tq_t,
 \qquad M_t=T(P)C_t. \tag{13}
\]
Then (12) is transported to
\[
 a(t)\cdot c=0\quad\Longrightarrow\quad c=M_tz
 \text{ for some }z\in\mathbb Z^r. \tag{14}
\]
A direct block multiplication, using (8), gives the important affine formula
\[
 M_t=tL(AW)-E=tD\,L(BW)-E, \tag{15}
\]
where \(E\) is a fixed integral matrix independent of \(t\). Here zero-sum lifting commutes with right multiplication: \(L(BW)=L(B)W\).

Put \(F=BW\). Cube admissibility survives the unimodular integral change of variables \(W\): if \(z\in\mathbb Z^r\) and \(\|L(F)z\|_\infty<1\), then \(Wz\in\mathbb Z^r\), \(\|L(B)(Wz)\|_\infty<1\), and hence \(Wz=0\), so \(z=0\).

Because \(F\) is nonsingular and the spaces are finite-dimensional, there is a constant \(K\ge0\), depending only on \(F\) and \(E\), such that
\[
 \|Ez\|_\infty\le K\|L(F)z\|_\infty \qquad(z\in\mathbb R^r). \tag{16}
\]
For example, write \(Ez=(EF^{-1})(Fz)\); the coordinates of \(Fz\) occur among those of \(L(F)z\), so an operator norm of \(EF^{-1}\) supplies such a \(K\).

For each \(k\), choose the least nonnegative integer \(t_k\) with
\[
 Dt_k\ge 2^k+K. \tag{17}
\]
Equivalently one may take \(t_k=\lceil(2^k+K)/D\rceil\). Then
\[
 \frac{t_k}{2^k}\longrightarrow\frac1D. \tag{18}
\]
We claim that \(a(t_k)\) is \(2^k\)-relation-free. Suppose
\[
 |c_i|<2^k\quad(0\le i\le r),\qquad a(t_k)\cdot c=0.
\]
By (14), \(c=M_{t_k}z\) for an integral \(z\). From (15), (16), and the reverse triangle inequality,
\[
 \begin{aligned}
 \|c\|_\infty
 &=\|Dt_kL(F)z-Ez\|_\infty\\
 &\ge (Dt_k-K)\|L(F)z\|_\infty\\
 &\ge 2^k\|L(F)z\|_\infty.
 \end{aligned} \tag{19}
\]
But \(\|c\|_\infty<2^k\), so \(\|L(F)z\|_\infty<1\). Cube admissibility of \(F\) gives \(z=0\), and consequently \(c=0\). This proves relation-freeness.

It remains to verify (7). The entries of \(q_t\) have degrees \(0,1,\dots,r\) in \(t\), and its last entry is
\[
 t^r\prod_i s_i.
\]
By the form of \(S(U)\), every entry of \(a(t)=S(U)^Tq_t\) is the last entry of \(q_t\), plus a fixed linear combination of its earlier entries. Therefore every coordinate of \(a(t)\) has the same leading term
\[
 t^r\prod_i s_i. \tag{20}
\]
Using (18), (9), and the fact that all lower powers disappear after division by \((2^k)^r\), we obtain
\[
 \frac{a_i(t_k)}{(2^k)^r}
 \longrightarrow
 \left(\frac1D\right)^r\prod_i s_i
 =|\det B|.
\]
This completes the proof of the transfer statement.

Now apply the binary-block estimate (3). Let \(\delta=|\det B|>0\). For all sufficiently large \(k\), all the integers \(a_i^{(k)}\) are positive and may be regarded as natural numbers. If \(C>\delta\), then for sufficiently large \(k\) every coordinate also satisfies
\[
 a_i^{(k)}<C(2^k)^r.
\]
Taking \(W_k=\max_i a_i^{(k)}\), estimate (3) says
\[
 C(2^k)^r<W_k,
\]
a contradiction. Thus every nonsingular cube-admissible rational matrix in every positive dimension would have to satisfy
\[
 C\le |\det B|. \tag{21}
\]
The same positive \(C\) works in all dimensions.

We next construct nonsingular cube-admissible rational matrices whose determinants are arbitrarily small, contradicting (21).

## 3. Odd-cycle gadgets

Let \(b\ge3\) be odd, and let \(P_b\) be the cyclic permutation matrix taking each coordinate to the following coordinate cyclically. Define
\[
 B_b=I+\frac12P_b. \tag{22}
\]
Since the eigenvalue/product identity for a cycle gives
\[
 \det(I+tP_b)=1+t^b\qquad(b\text{ odd}),

a first-row determinant expansion gives the same formula directly. Hence
\[
 \det B_b=1+2^{-b}. \tag{23}
\]

We require two elementary facts about short vectors under \(B_b\).

First, if all coordinates of \(B_bx\) have absolute value less than \(1\), then
\[
 |x_i|<2\quad\text{for every }i. \tag{24}
\]
Indeed, choose \(x_j\) of maximal absolute value and let \(x_{j-1}\) be its cyclic predecessor. Since
\[
 |x_j+\tfrac12x_{j-1}|<1,
\]
the triangle inequality gives
\[
 |x_j|<1+\tfrac12|x_{j-1}|\le1+\tfrac12|x_j|,
\]
which implies \(|x_j|<2\), and hence (24).

Second, suppose all coordinates except possibly \(x_0\) are integral and \(\|B_bx\|_\infty<1\). Then
\[
 \left|\sum_i x_i\right|<1. \tag{25}
\]
Here is the elementary chain argument. By (24), every integral coordinate is one of \(-1,0,1\). Along the nonclosing edges the inequalities are
\[
 |x_i+\tfrac12x_{i-1}|<1. \tag{26}
\]
If a preceding coordinate is zero, (26) forces the next integral coordinate to be zero. If both adjacent coordinates are in \(\{-1,0,1\}\) and the latter is nonzero, (26) forces the latter to be the negative of the former. Thus nonzero integral portions alternate in sign.

For completeness, one can track the partial sum without assuming \(x_0\) integral. After replacing \(x\) by \(-x\) if necessary, assume \(x_0\ge0\). An induction using the three possibilities \(-1,0,1\) in (26) shows that the sum of \(x_1,\dots,x_{b-1}\) is either \(0\), with \(x_{b-1}\ge0\), or \(-1\), with \(x_{b-1}\le0\). In the first case, the closing inequality
\[
 |x_0+\tfrac12x_{b-1}|<1
\]
implies \(|x_0|<1\), which is (25). In the second case, (24) gives \(0\le x_0<2\), so \(|x_0-1|<1\), again yielding (25). If \(x_0=0\), zero propagation makes all coordinates zero, and the same conclusion holds.

If all coordinates of \(x\) are integral, (24) places all of them in \(\{-1,0,1\}\). A nonzero short integral vector would have to alternate signs all the way around the cycle. On an odd cycle this is impossible: after an odd number of sign changes the closing edge requires a coordinate to be its own negative. Thus
\[
 x\in\mathbb Z^b,\quad \|B_bx\|_\infty<1
 \quad\Longrightarrow\quad x=0. \tag{27}
\]

We now make one determinant-one change of input coordinates. Let \(U_b\) leave coordinates \(1,\dots,b-1\) unchanged and set
\[
 (U_bx)_0=x_0-\sum_{i=1}^{b-1}x_i. \tag{28}
\]
This is an integral unipotent matrix, so \(\det U_b=1\), and
\[
 \sum_i(U_bx)_i=x_0. \tag{29}
\]
Set
\[
 H_b=B_bU_b. \tag{30}
\]
Then
\[
 \det H_b=1+2^{-b}. \tag{31}
\]
Moreover, because a cyclic permutation preserves coordinate sums,
\[
 \sum_i(B_by)_i=\frac32\sum_i y_i.
\]
Together with (29), this gives
\[
 \sum_i(H_bx)_i=\frac32x_0. \tag{32}
\]
The matrix \(H_b\) has two further properties:

1. If all \(x_i\) with \(i\ne0\) are integral and every coordinate of \(H_bx\) has absolute value less than \(1\), then \(|x_0|<1\). Indeed, apply (25) to \(U_bx\): its nonzero-index coordinates remain integral, and its coordinate sum is \(x_0\).

2. If all \(x_i\) are integral and \(\|H_bx\|_\infty<1\), then \(x=0\). This follows from (27), since \(U_b\) is an invertible integral transformation.

It is useful to package the properties needed for iteration. A cube gadget consists of a rational square matrix \(H\), a distinguished coordinate \(a\), and a positive rational number \(h\), with:

- \(\det H>0\);
- \(\sum_i(Hx)_i=h x_a\) for every rational vector \(x\);
- if all \(x_i\), \(i\ne a\), are integral and \(\|Hx\|_\infty<1\), then \(|x_a|<1\) (the strip property);
- if \(x\) is integral and \(\|Hx\|_\infty<1\), then \(x=0\) (integral admissibility).

The preceding discussion shows that, for every odd \(b\ge3\), \(H_b\) is a cube gadget with anchor \(0\), height
\[
 h=\frac32,
\]
and determinant \(1+2^{-b}\).

## 4. Composition of gadgets

Let \(G\) be a gadget on a finite set \(I\), and \(F\) one on a finite set \(J\). We construct a gadget on \(I\times J\). First apply \(G\) to the coordinates \((p,a_F)\), the anchor coordinate in every \(J\)-block, leaving all nonanchor coordinates unchanged. Then, independently in each block \(\{p\}\times J\), apply \(F\). Call the resulting matrix \(H_{G\circ F}\), and distinguish the coordinate \((a_G,a_F)\).

The height is the product \(h_Gh_F\). Indeed, summing within each child block multiplies its intermediate anchor by \(h_F\); summing those intermediate anchors and using the sum law for \(G\) then contributes \(h_G\).

The determinant is
\[
 \det H_{G\circ F}=\det H_G\,(\det H_F)^{|I|}. \tag{33}
\]
The first transformation is, after grouping all anchor coordinates together, block diagonal with blocks \(H_G\) and an identity matrix, so its determinant is \(\det H_G\). The second is block diagonal with \(|I|\) copies of \(H_F\), giving (33).

We verify that the two short-vector properties persist. Suppose all input coordinates except \((a_G,a_F)\) are integral and the final output is short. In each child block, all nonanchor inputs are integral. The strip property of \(F\) therefore says that the intermediate anchor in each block is short. These intermediate anchors are exactly the coordinates of the image under \(G\) of the original anchor inputs. All original anchor inputs except the distinguished one are integral, so the strip property of \(G\) gives that the distinguished input is short. This proves the strip property for the composite.

If the original input is entirely integral, the intermediate anchors are the image under \(G\) of an integral vector and, by the preceding child-strip argument, are all short. Admissibility of \(G\) forces all original anchor inputs to vanish. Consequently each child intermediate input is just the corresponding original integral block, and its output is short; admissibility of \(F\) kills every block. Thus the composite is integrally admissible.

Starting with the one-coordinate identity gadget and iterating the odd-cycle gadget \(H_b\) to depth \(k\), we obtain a gadget \(G_{b,k}\) with
\[
 b^k
\]
coordinates. Its height is
\[
 \left(\frac32\right)^k. \tag{34}
\]
If \(d_b=1+2^{-b}\), formula (33) gives the determinant recurrence
\[
 D_{b,0}=1,
 \qquad D_{b,k+1}=d_bD_{b,k}^{\,b}.
\]
Therefore
\[
 D_{b,k}=d_b^{E_{b,k}},
 \qquad
 E_{b,k}=1+b+\cdots+b^{k-1}. \tag{35}
\]

## 5. Extracting a cube-admissible minor

We now explain how any gadget with at least two coordinates produces a cube-admissible matrix of one smaller dimension.

Relabel coordinates so that the anchor is last. Suppose \(H\) is an \((r+1)\times(r+1)\) gadget matrix with height \(h\), and let \(B\) be the top-left \(r\times r\) minor obtained by deleting the anchor row and anchor column.

The sum law says that the sum of entries in every nonanchor column of \(H\) is zero, while the sum in the anchor column is \(h\). Replace the last row of \(H\) by the sum of all its rows. This row operation has determinant one. The resulting matrix has last row \((0,\dots,0,h)\), while its top-left block remains \(B\). Hence
\[
 \det H=h\det B. \tag{36}
\]
Since \(h>0\) and \(\det H>0\), \(B\) is nonsingular and \(\det B>0\), with
\[
 |\det B|=\frac{\det H}{h}. \tag{37}
\]

It remains to show that \(B\) is cube-admissible. Let \(z\in\mathbb Z^r\) satisfy
\[
 |(Bz)_i|<1\quad\text{for all }i,
 \qquad \left|\sum_i(Bz)_i\right|<1.
\]
Append a zero anchor coordinate to \(z\). The first \(r\) coordinates of the resulting \(H\)-image are \(Bz\). Its total coordinate sum is zero by the gadget sum law, since the anchor input is zero. Therefore its last coordinate is \(-\sum_i(Bz)_i\). All coordinates of the \(H\)-image are consequently of absolute value less than \(1\). Integral admissibility of the gadget forces the appended vector, and hence \(z\), to be zero. Thus \(B\) is cube-admissible.

Applying this to \(G_{b,k}\), where \(k>0\) and hence \(b^k\ge2\), yields a positive-dimensional nonsingular cube-admissible rational matrix \(B_{b,k}\) satisfying, by (34), (35), and (37),
\[
 |\det B_{b,k}|=
 \frac{(1+2^{-b})^{1+b+\cdots+b^{k-1}}}{(3/2)^k}. \tag{38}
\]

## 6. The determinants in (38) approach zero

We show that the right side of (38) can be made arbitrarily small. Let \(\varepsilon>0\). First choose a positive integer \(k\) so large that
\[
 \frac{2}{(3/2)^k}<\varepsilon. \tag{39}
\]
Keep this \(k\) fixed. Since
\[
 E_{b,k}=1+b+\cdots+b^{k-1}<b^k\qquad(b\ge2),
\]
and \(1+x\le e^x\), we have
\[
 (1+2^{-b})^{E_{b,k}}
 \le \exp(E_{b,k}2^{-b})
 \le \exp(b^k2^{-b}). \tag{40}
\]
For fixed \(k\), \(b^k2^{-b}\to0\) as \(b\to\infty\). Thus the right side of (40) tends to \(1\). We may consequently choose an odd \(b\ge3\) so large that
\[
 (1+2^{-b})^{E_{b,k}}<2. \tag{41}
\]
Equations (38), (39), and (41) then give
\[
 |\det B_{b,k}|<\varepsilon. \tag{42}
\]

Finally take \(\varepsilon=C\), where \(C>0\) is the supposed subset-sum constant. The matrix \(B_{b,k}\) is nonsingular, rational, cube-admissible, and positive-dimensional. The consequence (21) of the proposed subset-sum bound says
\[
 C\le|\det B_{b,k}|,
\]
whereas (42) says \(|\det B_{b,k}|<C\). This contradiction proves that no such positive constant \(C\) exists.

Therefore the asserted statement
\[
 \exists C>0\ \forall N,A:\quad
 A\subseteq\{1,\dots,N\},\ A\text{ sum-distinct},\ N\ne0
 \Longrightarrow C2^{|A|}<N
\]
is false.
